Does the ring differ from systemic methods in host gene expression? (Study B)

What this document is. The ring delivers contraceptive hormone locally; the pill and the injectable act systemically. If the local dose matters, the vaginal tissue under the ring should show a different host-transcriptome profile. This morning we start with an ordination of the genes to see the shape of the data before any test, then run a differential-expression analysis with DESeq2 comparing ring against the two systemic methods pooled. Full data QC lives in 01-qc.html; this document repeats only the checks this analysis depends on.

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(DESeq2)
library(microViz)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)      # PERMANOVA (adonis2)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)    # labels that do not overlap

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

d  <- read_counts("group_b")
ge <- d$genes          # 14,226 genes x 93 samples, RAW counts
md <- d$metadata       # one row per sample, same order as columns

# The two groups for the main question. Defined from the METADATA table,
# never from the count table we are about to test.
md <- md |> mutate(arm_group = if_else(arm == "ring", "ring", "systemic"))

1. QC for this analysis

stopifnot(identical(colnames(ge), md$sample_id))   # order check: DESeq2 would fail silently

batch_balance <- md |> dplyr::count(arm, rnaseq_batch) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rnaseq_batch, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
knitr::kable(batch_balance, caption = "Samples per arm and sequencing batch")
Samples per arm and sequencing batch
arm B1 B2
injectable 20 19
pill 14 14
ring 13 13
  • Order check passed: count-matrix columns and metadata rows are in the same sample_id order. DESeq2 does not warn if they differ — it would just be wrong.
  • Balance: every arm appears in both sequencing batches (ring 13/13, pill 14/14, injectable 20/19), so batch can go into the design as a covariate without confounding the contrast.
  • Carried flags from 01-qc.html: B093 carries heavy blood signal (about a third of its reads are HBB/HBA); B018/B029 lack cytokines (irrelevant here). Vaginal pH differs slightly across arms (p = 0.02) — a possible confounder to remember when reading results.

2. Ordination: do the samples separate by arm?

We keep genes with at least 10 reads in at least 10 samples, transform to CLR (centred log-ratio — log-ratios of each gene against the geometric mean of the sample, which is the standard way to handle compositional RNA-seq profiles in ordination), and draw a Euclidean PCoA.

ps_genes <- as_counts(dataset = "group_b", table = "rnaseq",
                      min_count = 10, min_samples = 10, data = d)
sd <- as(sample_data(ps_genes), "data.frame")
idx <- match(sd$sample_id, md$sample_id)
sd$arm       <- md$arm[idx]
sd$arm_group <- md$arm_group[idx]
sample_data(ps_genes) <- sample_data(sd)

ord <- ps_genes |>
  tax_transform("clr", zero_replace = "halfmin") |>
  dist_calc("euclidean") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

eig <- attr(ord, "ord")$CA$eig
sh  <- round(100 * eig / sum(eig), 1)

p_arm   <- ord_plot(ord, axes = 1:2, color = "arm") +
  labs(title = "By treatment arm", x = sprintf("Axis 1 (%s%%)", sh[1]),
       y = sprintf("Axis 2 (%s%%)", sh[2]), color = "Arm")
p_batch <- ord_plot(ord, axes = 1:2, color = "rnaseq_batch") +
  labs(title = "By sequencing batch", x = sprintf("Axis 1 (%s%%)", sh[1]),
       y = NULL, color = "Batch")
p_arm + p_batch
# PERMANOVA: does the distance between samples depend on arm / batch?
# Same CLR+Euclidean distances as the plot above.
dm <- attr(ord, "dist")
meta_p <- sd[rownames(as.matrix(dm)), ]
set.seed(1)
per_arm   <- adonis2(dm ~ arm_group, data = meta_p, permutations = 999)
per_batch <- adonis2(dm ~ rnaseq_batch, data = meta_p, permutations = 999)

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    term     = c("arm_group", "rnaseq_batch"),
    R2_pct   = round(100 * c(per_arm$R2[1], per_batch$R2[1]), 1),
    p_value  = c(per_arm$`Pr(>F)`[1], per_batch$`Pr(>F)`[1])
  ),
  caption = "PERMANOVA on CLR + Euclidean distances (999 permutations)"
)
PERMANOVA on CLR + Euclidean distances (999 permutations)
term R2_pct p_value
arm_group 1.7 0.040
rnaseq_batch 1.4 0.107 
n_kept <- nrow(otu_table(ps_genes))

The gene table keeps 14221 of 14,226 genes after the filter. The ordination plot shows no separation by arm that the eye can pick up, but PERMANOVA — which tests whether sample-to-sample distances depend on a variable, using permutation p-values — puts a small but real 1.7 % of the variation on arm_group (p = 0.040), while sequencing batch accounts for a similar 1.4 % that is not significant (p = 0.107). That is the honest first answer to this morning’s question: the ring’s effect on the overall host-expression profile is subtle — detectable by a permutation test, not by looking at the map. Individual genes may still shift clearly, which is what DESeq2 tests next.

Sanity check. The share of variation on axis 1 is printed in the axis title. Recompute it by hand: run the PCA-free version by asking for adonis2’s R2 for arm_group — it should match the table above, because both come from the same distance matrix.

3. Differential expression: ring vs systemic

DESeq2 models raw counts (it does its own size-factor normalisation and dispersion shrinkage). Never give it CPM or logged values.

genes_f <- ge[rowSums(ge >= 10) >= 10, ]     # same filter as the ordination
rownames(md) <- md$sample_id

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(genes_f, md, design = ~ rnaseq_batch + arm_group)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("arm_group", "ring", "systemic"))

res_df <- as.data.frame(res) |>
  rownames_to_column("ensembl_gene_id") |>
  left_join(d$gene_info |> select(ensembl_gene_id, symbol),
            by = "ensembl_gene_id") |>
  mutate(symbol = coalesce(symbol, ensembl_gene_id),
         padj   = replace_na(padj, 1))

sig <- res_df |> filter(padj < 0.05)
knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    quantity = c("genes tested", "FDR < 0.05", "up in ring (FDR < 0.05)",
                 "down in ring (FDR < 0.05)", "smallest FDR"),
    value = c(nrow(res_df), nrow(sig),
              sum(sig$log2FoldChange > 0), sum(sig$log2FoldChange < 0),
              format(min(res_df$padj), digits = 2))
  ),
  caption = "DESeq2 results, ring vs systemic"
)
DESeq2 results, ring vs systemic
quantity value
genes tested 14221
FDR < 0.05 165
up in ring (FDR < 0.05) 88
down in ring (FDR < 0.05) 77
smallest FDR 2.6e-09

4. What do the hits look like?

res_df |>
  mutate(hit = padj < 0.05,
         label = if_else(rank(padj) <= 10, symbol, NA_character_)) |>
  ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = hit)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey70", "firebrick")) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 2.8, max.overlaps = 20,
                  show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change (ring vs systemic)",
       y = "-log10 adjusted p-value")
top <- sig |> slice_min(padj, n = 15) |>
  transmute(symbol, log2FC = round(log2FoldChange, 2),
            FDR = signif(padj, 2))
knitr::kable(top, caption = "15 smallest-FDR genes, ring vs systemic")

top_gene <- sig |> slice_min(padj, n = 1) |> pull(ensembl_gene_id)
plot_df  <- md |>
  mutate(counts = ge[top_gene, ]) |>
  mutate(arm_group = factor(arm_group, c("systemic", "ring")))
ggplot(plot_df, aes(arm_group, counts + 0.5, colour = arm_group)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = str_c("Raw counts of ", top$symbol[1], " (top hit)"),
       x = NULL, y = "raw counts (+0.5, log10)")

Sanity check. Take the top hit’s raw counts, average them within ring and within systemic, and divide the two means — the ratio, converted to log2, should be close to the log2FC in the table above (DESeq2’s estimate shrinks a little, so near rather than exact).

5. Sensitivity: does B093 drive the result?

B093’s blood signal could masquerade as a ring effect if it happened to sit in one arm. We refit without it and count how many of the main hits survive.

md_s <- md |> filter(sample_id != "B093")
dds_s <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(genes_f[, md_s$sample_id], md_s,
                                design = ~ rnaseq_batch + arm_group)
dds_s <- DESeq(dds_s)
res_s <- results(dds_s, contrast = c("arm_group", "ring", "systemic")) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("ensembl_gene_id")

survive <- sig |>
  inner_join(res_s |> filter(padj < 0.05), by = "ensembl_gene_id")

Of the 165 genes significant in the main fit, 152 remain significant at FDR < 0.05 after dropping B093 (92% survival). Low survival would mean the top hits lean on one blood-contaminated sample; high survival means the result is spread across samples.

6. Verdict

  • The gene-table ordination shows no separation by arm that the eye can see, but PERMANOVA finds arm_group explains a small, significant share of the variation (1.7 %, p = 0.04); sequencing batch is similar in size (1.4 %) and not significant.
  • DESeq2 finds 165 genes at FDR < 0.05 for ring vs systemic (88 up in ring). Inspect the top hits’ biology before believing any single one — with 14221 genes tested, hits at the FDR boundary deserve replication or an independent check.
  • The result survives dropping B093 at the rate reported above, so it does not hinge on the one blood-contaminated sample.
  • Overall: any ring-vs-systemic difference in host expression is modest. This matches the ordination: nothing dramatic, the kind of signal that needs the cytokine and microbiome angles (and the workshop’s other datasets) before it becomes a claim.

Choices made

  • Pooled the two systemic methods into one systemic group for the main contrast; testing ring vs pill and ring vs injectable separately is the alternative and would answer a slightly different question.
  • Checked the pooling assumption by eye via the three-arm ordination rather than a formal pill-vs-injectable test; a formal test is the alternative.
  • Used raw counts in DESeq2 with ~ rnaseq_batch + arm_group — batch as a covariate because both arms appear in both batches; an interaction term (~ rnaseq_batch * arm_group) is the alternative but spends degrees of freedom we would rather keep.
  • Filtered genes at ≥ 10 reads in ≥ 10 samples (same filter for ordination and DESeq2) — a stricter rule loses power, a laxer one wastes tests on near-empty genes; independent filtering is also handled inside DESeq2 itself.
  • CLR + Euclidean for the gene ordination, because gene profiles are compositional like the species table; Aitchison on a filtered table and Bray-Curtis on raw counts were the alternatives.
  • No log2-fold-change shrinkage (apeglm/ashr are not installed here); unshrunken LFCs are reported, which can exaggerate fold changes for low-count genes — the top table should be read with that in mind.
  • FDR < 0.05 across all tested genes; a fold-change threshold on top (e.g. |LFC| > 1) is the alternative and would shrink the hit list further.
  • Kept B093 in the main fit (it is quantitatively, not catastrophically, unusual) and ran a sensitivity analysis without it instead of dropping it outright; dropping it from the start would be the alternative.
  • Report unadjusted p-values nowhere; everything shown is FDR-adjusted.
